title: Help or Rescue
concept: After this one you can tell helping from saving, so you stop doing other people's part of the work.
bookIdea: Steiner says you are rescuing when you do something for someone that you don't really want to do or when you put in more than half of the effort, and his rules for avoiding a rescue add that you should not help without a request or a contract, so any one of the three is enough.

opener.setting: Monday, 7:20am, Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B, the kitchen. The milk is in the fridge door and the bread is nearly gone.

lines.text: “Morning! You're a legend, you know that? Could you grab my lunch box off the counter? I'm already late.”
lines.cue: half into his shoes, phone wedged under his chin

lines.text: “It's fine. I'm going past the gate anyway.”
lines.cue: not looking up from the bread

opener.ask: Which of these acts are helping, and which are saving?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Helping leaves the other person their share, and saving takes it. Three checks tell them apart: someone asked, you want to do it, and you are doing no more than half. If any one check fails, it is saving.

items.text: “Sam's share of the electricity is short again. I've covered the gap from my account. Don't tell him, he's had a bad month.”
items.cue: stirring the lentils, back to you
items.why: Nobody asked Maya to pay Sam's bill, and she hid it from him. She is also carrying all of his share. That is saving, and the gap will open again next month with Maya alone to fill it.

traps.0: Helping. It sounds kind, and the bill is paid. But nobody asked her to pay, and Sam never learns there was a bill, so the gap comes back next month.

items.example:
Family WhatsApp group, Sunday night.
Uncle Mark: “I've booked the cab for Gran's check-up, don't argue.”
Cousin: “Oh, I was going to sort that.”
Uncle Mark: “Too late now.”

items.text: “Can you read the second slide? Just that one. I'll fix the rest myself.”
items.cue: laptop balanced on her knees on the stairs
items.why: She asked for one slide and said she would do the rest. Reading that slide and saying what is unclear is help she can use, and the rest stays hers.

traps.1: Saving. It sounds like pitching in, but she asked for one slide. Taking the whole deck would be more than half the work, and she would walk into the demo knowing nothing about her own slides.

items.example:
Central station, platform 1, 7:40am.
Man: “Is this the train to the coast? Just tell me that.”
You: “Yes, that's the one.”
He thanks you and walks off to find the coach himself.

items.text: “Leave the pipeline with me. I'll fix it, write the notes and tell the client.”
items.cue: Omar had only asked you to look at one failing test
items.why: Omar asked for one test. You took the whole pipeline, the notes and the client call, which is more than half the work. That is saving. Omar gets a fixed build and none of the skill.

traps.0: Helping. His back gets a rest, and the build works. But you have taken more than half the work for one failing test, and next time Omar won't even ask.

items.example:
Badminton club, Saturday, 7:00am.
Captain: “Could you bring the net? Just the net.”
You: “I'll bring the net and set up the courts.”
Captain: “Wow. Thanks.” Next week the courts are yours by default.

items.text: “Hear my spellings? Don't tell me the answer, okay?”
items.cue: holding the card upside down so he can't peek
items.why: He asked for a listener and set the rules himself. You say the word and wait while he spells it. The spelling stays his, and so does the learning.

traps.1: Saving. Spelling the words for him would be doing the whole task, more than half of it, and he would learn that the answers come from grown-ups, not from his own head.

items.example:
Tuition class, Tuesday, 5:30pm.
Teacher: “Read the passage to yourself first.”
Girl: “Can you read it to me? I'll tell you when I get stuck.”
Teacher: “Good. Start, and I'll wait.”

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Now the options look alike. Run the checks one at a time: did anyone ask, do you want to do it, and who is carrying more than half?

items.text: “I need the pricing section for the client deck by Thursday. You know it best. Can you take it?”
items.cue: tapping his laptop lid, already turning back to his screen. Last month you told him you dread pricing.
options: Saving: you do what you don't want to
items.why: He asked, and he asked for one section, so the 'nobody asked' check and the 'more than half' check both pass. You dread pricing and said yes anyway. The check that fails is the one about wanting to do it.

traps.0: Helping. He asked, and you said yes, so it looks like a favour. But you dread the pricing slides, and that dread turns into a short reply to his next email.
traps.1: Saving: more than half. Only one section of the deck is yours, so this check passes. Calling it that would make Daniel feel he has handed you the whole job.
traps.3: Saving: nobody asked. He did ask, and he asked you by name. This answer would turn a plain request into an accusation in his own project.

items.example:
Parents' WhatsApp group, Thursday night.
Ella: “Can someone do the snacks for Saturday? Only one of you, please.”
Mei: “I'll do them. I hate baking, but fine.”
Ella: “Lovely.” Mei bakes until midnight and says nothing.

items.text: “Could you help me with the cupboard? Just the top shelf. My knees are not what they were.”
items.cue: steel plate in her hand, watching you carry the boxes down
options: Saving: you do what you don't want to
items.why: She asked for the top shelf. You emptied the whole cupboard and carried everything down, which is more than half the work. That check fails, and she watched from the chair.

traps.0: Helping. She did ask, and she is grateful. But the top shelf turned into the whole cupboard, and she never learns to do it herself.
traps.2: Saving: you do what you don't want to. Nothing in the scene says you minded the boxes, so this check passes. Saying it would make her feel like a burden.
traps.3: Saving: nobody asked. She did ask, for the top shelf. This answer misses the real point, which is that you did far more than she asked for.

items.example:
Market by the bus stop, Saturday, 8:30am.
Vendor: “Can you hold the scale while I weigh the onions?”
You: “Sure. I'll bag them and carry them to your van.”
Vendor: “Good. Thank you.” His son stays on the crate with a sausage roll.

items.text: “Could you read my cover letter tonight? I've written it and cut it twice. I just need a second pair of eyes.”
items.cue: holding out her phone at the bus stop, thumb already on the draft. You like tidying other people's sentences.
options: Saving: you do what you don't want to
items.why: She asked, she wrote the letter herself, and you enjoy this kind of job. You flag two sentences that drag and send it back. All three checks pass, so this is plain helping.

traps.1: Saving: more than half. It would be if you rewrote the letter. But she asked for a read, she did the writing, and your share is two comments.
traps.2: Saving: you do what you don't want to. Nothing in the scene says you mind. You like this job, so that check passes.
traps.3: Saving: nobody asked. She asked you directly, and she named the job. That check passes too.

items.example:
Garden fence, Sunday, 10:00am.
Neighbour: “Could you hold the ladder while I fix the gutter? I'll do the climbing.”
You: “Happy to.” He climbs, you steady the ladder, and you both have tea afterwards.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Time for the book's word. Steiner calls saving a rescue. First explain one, then sort four more acts from the flat.

items.text: “Sam's late again. I've covered his share, so the flat doesn't have to fight. It's easier for everyone.”
options: Helping: the flat stays calm, and that is what a good flatmate does.
A rescue. Nobody asked Maya to pay, and she is carrying all of Sam's share, so his lateness never becomes his problem. Helping would be to tell Sam the number and leave the payment with him.
Not a rescue. Maya can afford it and doesn't mind, and Steiner counts it as a rescue only when you do something you don't want to do.
items.why: Two checks fail at once: nobody asked, and Maya is doing more than half, since she carries the whole share. Any one failure is enough. The cheque also keeps Sam's lateness going, because he never feels what it costs.

traps.0: Helping: the flat stays calm, and calm is good. But Maya pays for that calm, and Sam never feels what being late costs him.
traps.2: Not a rescue. Steiner names more than one way into a rescue, and failing any of them is enough. A willing payer still rescues if nobody asked and she carries the whole share.

items.example:
Office canteen, 1:10pm.
Colleague: “I'll get the tea today. You can get the next round.”
You: “Thanks.”
Nobody checks who got the last three rounds, and the colleague starts treating it as the arrangement.

items.prompt: Four more acts from the flat. Put each one where Steiner's checks place it.
bins: Saving: you do what you don't want to

items.text: Sam asks Maya to check one clause in the lease about the deposit. She reads it, tells him what it means, and he writes the email himself.
items.why: He asked, she wanted to, and her part was small. The email stays his, so every check passes.

items.text: Sam is out. Maya tidies his room and sorts his post into piles. He never asked, and she enjoys tidying.
items.why: She likes the job, so the 'want to' check passes. But nobody asked, and help that starts without a request takes over a space that was his.

items.text: Sam asks for help with the budget sheet. Maya builds every tab, sets up the formulas and sends it back finished.
items.why: He asked, and she was glad to. But she did all of the work, so the sheet is hers and Sam learns nothing about his own money.

items.text: Sam asks if she'll come to his cousin's cricket final. She finds cricket dull and he can see it, but she says she'd love to.
items.why: He asked, and she gave a small share of her day. The failing check is that she went along with something she didn't want to do, afraid he'd be hurt if she said no.

items.example:
Book group, Friday, 7:30pm.
Host: “Could someone bring the wine?”
You: “I'll bring wine, cook the starter and wash up.”
Host: “Lovely.” Next month it is the same, and nobody else offers.

debrief.nadia: Most help feels kind on the day you give it. Saving shows up weeks later, as a bill nobody signed and a person who never got the chance to learn what it costs. Before your hands move, ask who asked and whether you actually want to. Then ask whose half you are quietly taking.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a rescue. Steiner's two signs of one are doing something for someone that you don't want to do and putting in more than half of the effort. He adds that you should not help without a request, and he counts holding back what you want from someone as a rescue too.

reflection.prompt: What did you do for someone this week that nobody asked for? What did it cost you, and what did they never get the chance to learn for themselves?
